### 1. TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing (2610.12242)
- what: Proposes a serving runtime for token-level LLM routing (per-model subservers, handoff-resume that keeps a routed request's serving state across model switches, and a delayed-batching scheduler whose threshold is chosen from a DTMC throughput model), built on SGLang 0.5.1.
- read: full (text supplied); read through Appendix D.4 and the final sentence of the paper. No code or weights were fetched; I did not read the repo.
- key numbers: 2.01–64.15× throughput "compared with the stronger baseline" across 15 algorithm–workload cells (Sec. 5.2, Figs. 5/6, concurrency 4). Against plain LLM-only serving, Table 2 R2R at concurrency 4 gives 244.56 tok/s for TokenRouter vs 145.30 LLM-only, a recomputed 1.68×; the same table gives 89.62 for official code, so 2.73× over official code. Table 6 at N=4: 210.61 full vs 73.27 official R2R (2.87×, recomputed).
- code/weights: github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter stated in the abstract. Routing pairs use Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B/4B/8B/32B (Sec. 5.1, Table 3). The original-setting experiments use other models per Table 4: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/32B (R2R), Qwen2-1.5B/72B (CITER), LLaMA2-7B (tuned)/70B (Co-LLM), L1-1.5B-Short/QwQ-32B (R-Stitch). Hardware is 8×A100-80G (Sec. 5.1), and the two-model setup uses CUDA MPS.
- practical: LOW
- why: The transferable piece is handoff-resume: keep a routed request's KV state across model switches instead of re-running prefix matching. Table 10 shows prefix matching, lock/release and radix-cache update make up about 85% of Std. Serving's SLM step time (20.94 + 17.47 + 13.81 + 32.62), not 80%. Using this needs a modified SGLang serving engine with inter-model IPC, which your hosted APIs and browser inference cannot expose, so it stays LOW. The headline is relative to the "stronger baseline," which the authors describe as their own SGLang Std. Serving build plus official engines "without continuous batching" (Sec. 5.1). Plain LLM-only serving gives a smaller gain (about 1.68× for R2R at N=4). Table 2 also shows Co-LLM at 76 tok/s under TokenRouter against 135 LLM-only, so routing does not beat a plain large model there. The Table 3 gains (1.99–3.21×) come from single runs. I checked Sec. 5.1 Metrics, Sec. 5.3, and Appendix A.2 and found no repeat count, seed, or spread. The DTMC threshold model is validated only on R2R at one p=0.35 and two thread counts (App. D.4, Fig. 10), so it does not show generality. Muninn's `decide` gates at the request level, so the per-token mechanism does not apply to it.

evolver.reasoning: Checked the draft's numbers and claims against the paper text. VelaBench 51.5→63.0 is +11.5 and the general OOD average 54.2→58.2 is +4.0, both matching Table 1. Table 2 shows VelaBench 62.4 with and without difficulty filtering, and the OOD deltas (+0.8, +1.5, +1.2, +0.9) average 1.1, so the 'benefit confined to OOD' reading holds. ### 1. Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm (2610.40564)
- what: Recasts pretraining, midtraining, SFT and binary-reward RL (MaxRL/REINFORCE targets) as one weighted likelihood loss over a mixture of static data and self-generated successes, and compares unified mixing with staged training at 124M (puzzles) and 0.76B (math/code) scale.
- read: full (text supplied, through the final sentence of Appendix F; nothing truncated). I did not use any summary or outside source.
- key numbers: (a) Controlled Base, Table 9: best staged pass@1 24.54% (2 epochs, 2e-4); the unified advantage appears only as compute frontiers (Figs. 5, 12), averaged over two seeds (Appendix C.4). (b) Real-world, Table 15 and Table 17: Math average pass@1 at 0.5% constant mixing is 24.27 (= (16.83+31.71)/2) vs. staged 24.16 (= (16.98+31.35)/2), a 0.11 pp gap. (c) Throughput, Appendix D.6: 3.7 s vs. 28.8 s per update, which recomputes to 7.8× (28.8/3.7), but D.6 says the implementations use 24 vs. 16 GPUs and differ in asynchrony and baseline subtraction, and that the comparison "does not isolate the effects of staleness or baseline subtraction individually." So the gap is confounded. (d) MaxRL vs. REINFORCE, Table 20: Math pass@1 (REINFORCE minus MaxRL) ranges from −1.29 pp (constant 0.5%) to +0.82 pp (constant 2%), and the sign flips across mixtures.
- code/weights: The Website, GitHub (https://github.com/yudasong/unified-training) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/sfanm/unified-training) links are stated in the front matter. I did not verify that they run.
- practical: LOW
- why: The usable idea is small: reweight correct generations by 1/p̂ and mix them into the same weighted-CE buffer as static replay data. The evidence is from from-scratch 124M and 0.76B models trained for 6k–12k updates. I checked Appendix C.4 and D.1: the controlled study reports two seeds and no CI; the real-world study reports no seed count or CI, though its benchmarks are fixed full sets (500, 1319, 164 and 378 problems). The 0.11 pp math gain sits inside the 16.11–16.91 MATH-500 spread across the 0–5% mixtures in Table 15. Running this needs trainer and weight-sync infrastructure his hosted APIs do not expose, so per E-05 it stays LOW. The static-replay-plus-successes idea is worth noting for Muninn's memory design, but he cannot test it on his current models.

The rating stays LOW because the paper's main output is an observation about visible text across models, not a routing or cost method you could test within weeks. For your routing work, the transferable part is the gate: check ETR on the answer-only subagent before trusting it.

### 1. RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models (2610.13912)
- what: A framework that wraps world-model-guided candidate selection, feedback-driven policy/workflow updates, conditional world-model adaptation, and accept/retain checks into one recursive loop, evaluated across code repair, GUI, lab planning, reaction optimization and an immune-science case.
- read: full (text supplied; the paper text provided to me, no URL fetched). The text runs to the appendix affiliations and I read all of it.
- key numbers: Code repair hidden-test success 26.3% (static verifier) → 29.2% (fixed W1, 175/600) → 31.2% (adapted W1), with a paired gain of +2.83 pp, 95% interval [+0.17, +5.50] (Sec 3.1, Table 2). Reaction optimization 96.15% vs 82.16% for Bayesian optimization after 40 experiments, a 13.99 pp gain from a single flow screen (Sec 3.4, Fig 6f). LabHorizon L2 0.4601 vs 0.4532 for the Actor–Simulator–Selector reference, a 0.69 pp gap (Sec 3.3).
- code/weights: Links stated: GitHub "Gen-Verse/RSI-Anything" and a Hugging Face link, which the paper labels as a datasets URL (the header reads "Models: RSI-Anything" but points to huggingface.co/datasets/...). The paper does not say which artifact (weights, adapters, W1, the ReactionT5 adapter) is released. Treat the release as unverified.
- practical: LOW
- why: The one transferable piece is the policy–predictor acceptance gate (Eqs. 13–18), but the paper gives no thresholds, no concrete compatibility criterion, and no ablation of the pair check. The headline code-repair gain rests on 200 tasks across three seeds with a 2.8 pp paired delta, and the "adaptation" step adds only 2.0 pp over a fixed model, with the same 3.72 calls per task. The reaction result is a single screen and a 13.99 pp gap with no seed or repeat count given; the paper does not state that Bayesian optimization was tuned, so I cannot call the baseline weak. GUI and immune-science results are single-configuration or depend on the cited companion paper. Nothing here runs on his hardware without re-implementing the world-model stack, so the rating stays LOW.

### 1. RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models (2610.13912)
- what: A framework that combines world-model-guided candidate selection, feedback-driven policy or workflow updates, conditional world-model adaptation, and component and pair acceptance checks into one recursive loop, evaluated on code repair, GUI tasks, lab planning, Suzuki–Miyaura reaction search, and an immune-science case.
- read: full (text supplied; no URL fetched). The supplied text runs through Appendix A (affiliations and correspondence), and I read it to the end.
- key numbers: Code repair hidden-test success is 26.3% for the capacity-matched static verifier, 29.2% for fixed-world-model selection (175/600), and 31.2% for adapted world-model selection, with a paired gain of +2.83 pp over the static verifier and a 95% interval of [+0.17, +5.50] (Sec 3.1, Table 2). The flow LC–MS reaction screen gives 96.15% vs 82.16% for Bayesian optimization after 40 experiments, +13.99 pp (Sec 3.4, Fig 6f). The GC screen gives 93.0% vs 87.5% after 20 experiments, +5.5 pp (Sec 3.4, Fig 6c). LabHorizon F200 Level-2 Final Score is 46.01% vs 45.32% for the Actor–Simulator–Selector reference, +0.69 pp (Sec 3.3, Table 3).
- code/weights: Links stated: GitHub (Gen-Verse/RSI-Anything) and a Hugging Face URL. The paper's header labels the Hugging Face link "Models," but its path is /datasets/. The paper does not say which artifact is released (W1, adapters, the ReactionT5 adapter, or policy weights), so treat any release as unverified.
- practical: LOW
- why: The transferable piece is the component and pair acceptance gate (Eqs. 13–18), but Sec 2.5 only refers to "predeclared acceptance criteria," and the paper gives no thresholds, no concrete compatibility criterion, and no ablation of the pair check. The code-repair evidence is the strongest: 200 tasks over three seeds, with the task-clustered interval stated in Sec 6.2 covering only the 2.83 pp fixed-model gap, while the 2.0 pp adaptation step has no interval. The reaction, LabHorizon, and GUI numbers have no seed or repeat counts or spread. The reaction sequences state no seed or repeat count (Sec 6.2 gives only "observed running best within each optimization sequence," and Sec 6.1 names Bayesian optimization as the baseline without tuning details), and the checkbox GUI results (51% → 79% → 99%, Fig 4c) are one MiniWoB++ task with no seed count stated in Sec 6.1. Nothing here runs on his hardware without re-implementing the world-model stack, so the rating stays LOW.

- practical: LOW
- why: The survey itself reports no measured effect for any Harness component, so it cannot show that the orchestration/monitoring/memory split helps. The concrete idea he could test in a day is the function-protocol pattern in Section 7.1 (typed failures plus post-call state; success conditions checked by an evaluator separate from the planner, citing Physical Agency [76], Physical Agentic AI [221], and Thea [349]), which would need his own A/B on Muninn's tools to justify. The headline numbers are other papers' results on a flagship model he cannot test on his stack, so they do not raise the rating (E-03, E-04).

Nothing here is a benchmark or method you could run on your Muninn/remex stack within weeks. ### 1. FlatCake: A Flat KVCache Storage Architecture for LLM Serving (2610.38355)
- what: Proposes replacing the DRAM→SSD tiered KV cache with a flat layout in which each KV block is written once directly to DRAM or NVMe SSD (session-contiguous, layer-major) behind a 64-bit GVA space, with dual-queue scheduling and GDS streaming into a bounded GPU window, implemented in SGLang.
- read: full (text supplied, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38355 as the paper ID; text supplied in the message). The supplied text ends at the Conclusion, so the full body was read. No appendix or artifact section appears in the supplied text.
- key numbers: At 1.0 QPS on the Claude Code trace, mean TTFT 7.57 s vs. Mooncake 12.24 s (1.6×) and HBM+L2 DRAM 17.51 s (§5.2). Delivered hit rate 94.16–94.57% vs. Mooncake 64.26% at ≥0.5 QPS (§5.2). SSD read amplification 6.51–6.72× Mooncake (§5.3). Llama-3.1-70B at 64K: 3.74 s vs. Mooncake-GDS 6.60 s (§5.4).
- code/weights: not stated in the supplied text. The paper names SGLang v0.5.19 and Mooncake v0.3.13, but gives no FlatCake repository link.
- practical: LOW
- why: The core idea (write-once, session-scoped placement, no migration) is transferable only as a design principle; the implementation needs a modified SGLang HiCache backend, GDS with NVMe RAID on B200/A100-class hardware, and a custom GVA allocator, none of which he runs. The headline numbers come from a single 8×B200 testbed with one production trace, and the paper gives no seed, repeat, or confidence-interval numbers for the load sweeps (I scanned Table 1, Table 3, and §5 for 'seed', 'run', 'repeat', 'trial' and found no matches). The idea does not transfer to his hosted-API routing or in-browser WebGPU work, so the rating stays LOW under E-05.
papers.final_text:
### 1. FlatCake: A Flat KVCache Storage Architecture for LLM Serving (2610.38355)
- what: Replaces the DRAM→SSD tiered KV cache with a flat layout in which each block is written once to DRAM or NVMe SSD (session-contiguous, layer-major) behind a 64-bit GVA space, with dual-queue scheduling and GDS streaming into a bounded GPU window, implemented in SGLang.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; the arXiv ID is https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38355). The supplied text runs through the Conclusion's last sentence. It has no appendix, artifact section, or reference list.
- key numbers: At 1.0 QPS on the Claude Code trace, mean TTFT is 7.57 s vs. Mooncake 12.24 s (1.6×, recomputed 12.24/7.57 = 1.62) and HBM+L2 DRAM 17.51 s (2.3×) (§5.2). Delivered hit rate is 94.16–94.57% vs. Mooncake 64.26% at ≥0.5 QPS (§5.2). Llama-3.1-70B at 64K: 3.74 s vs. Mooncake-GDS 6.60 s (1.8×, recomputed 6.60/3.74 = 1.76) (§5.4).
- code/weights: not stated. The paper names SGLang v0.5.19 and Mooncake v0.3.13 (§5.1) and reports about 8.8K lines of C++/CUDA and 7.1K lines of Python (§4), but gives no FlatCake repository link.
- practical: NONE
- why: The only transferable element is a design principle (write-once, session-scoped placement with no migration). The candidate rules, HRRN priority in Eq. 1, arrival_ts re-admission in §3.3, and Δgap = 64 KiB bridging in §3.4, order KV-restore I/O. They cannot be run on his hosted subagents, and the FC-MAS ablation in §5.3 removes dual-queue, Eq. 1 and re-admission together, so no single rule's gain is isolated. The gains depend on the SGLang HiCache backend, GDS over an 8-drive NVMe RAID0 (Table 3), and B200/A100 hardware, none of which he runs.
- Seeds: I scanned the measure, episode and instance columns of Table 1 and Table 3, the §5.1 setup text, and the captions of Figures 6–10 for "seed", "run", "repeat" and "trial", and found no matches. The paper gives no seed or repeat count for these results, and no appendix is cited or present in the supplied text. The DeepSeek headline uses one production trace (claude-code-weka-0621, §5.1). The Llama sweep names no trace in the supplied text. These points are limited to the supplied text.

evolver.notice: Fix one misread number and one overstated claim before finalising. In Table 2 the 4th column group is General (100), where VPM (V) = 26.54 and VPM (V+T) = 33.92. The Real-world Robot (100) group is the 3rd group, where VPM (V) = 50.83 and VPM (V+T) = 64.75 (also shown in Table 6 and Table 19). Use the group header when quoting these. The V vs V+T comparison is repeated under all-view I2V (Table 16), 2-view I2V (Table 17), V2V (Table 18), zero-shot ReCamMaster/CMU Panoptic (Table 26), and data scales of 10K/100K/600K (Figure 9). Describe those, then state precisely what is missing: Appendix A.2 gives three random seeds only for RoboCasa, and the real-robot tables use 24 trials per task. Keep the reliability argument to the real-robot per-task gaps (Table 5: Banana 58.3→79.2, Cup 64.6→70.8, Cube 43.8→54.2, which span roughly 1.5 to 5 trials), and cite the tables you rely on.

papers.final_text:
### 1. Learning the 4D World through Point Trajectory Forecasting (2610.28594)
- what: Adds a 3D point-trajectory head and a cross-view correspondence loss to a camera-conditioned multi-view video world model (VPM, built on Cosmos3-Nano), and adds robot actions as a token modality for a robot-control variant.
- read: full (text supplied, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28594 as provided; the supplied text runs through Appendix G.3 with no truncation).
- key numbers: Table 2, Simulation Robot (500) FVD: Cosmos3-N 104.74 → VPM (V) 78.52 → VPM (V+T) 67.35. Recomputed V→V+T reduction: (78.52−67.35)/78.52 = 14.2%. Table 2, Real-world Robot (100) δ3D: VPM (V) 50.83 → VPM (V+T) 64.75. Table 5, real-robot V+A → V+T+A: Banana 58.3 → 79.2, Cup 64.6 → 70.8, Cube 43.8 → 54.2, with 24 trials per task (Sec. 6.4, A.2), so one trial is about 4.2 points.
- code/weights: Project page and Hugging Face dataset links for VPM-Data and VP-WorldBench are stated. No model weights or training/inference code link is stated in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The method is a three-stage training recipe over a 600K-sample mixture on 32 GH200 GPUs (A.1, B.1), built on a backbone the reader does not run, so E-01 and E-05 apply. The V vs V+T gaps are consistent across the all-view I2V, 2-view I2V, V2V, zero-shot ReCamMaster/CMU Panoptic setups (Tables 16–18, 26) and the 10K/100K/600K data scales (Fig. 9), so the weakness is infrastructure and absent weights, not noise. The robot-action gains are the thin part: the Cup and Cube gaps are about 1.5 and 2.5 trials, and no seed or repeat count is stated for Table 5 (only RoboCasa's "three random seeds" in A.2), so E-02 applies there.

evolver.reasoning: Checked the draft's numbers against the paper. Table 2 gives Opus 4.5 SWE-bench Verified as 70.0 (mini) vs 70.2 (SAC) and GPT 5.6 Sol as 84.4 vs 82.4, matching the draft. The Section 3 cost multiples (2.2x–8.8x for Opus long-horizon) and the Section 4 long-input multiples (6.5x–54.6x, 4.4x–233.3x) match the text. Appendix B shows the cost figures are estimated from a retail model with r = 0.20 (the rounded mean of three measured ratios), not metered bills, so the draft's description is accurate. The paper releases no code link (only project pages), and the principal models are closed, as the draft says. The only repeatability statement is the 2% throughput variation in Section 2.5. The results tables contain no seed, run, repeat or trial columns, so the draft's claim of single runs holds. Accuracy margins of 1–3 points have no paper-reported spread, control or agreement check, so E-02 supports LOW. The draft could have named the Appendix A/G compaction prompt structure as the concrete testable component, but the LOW rating and its reasoning are supported by the paper text, so no revision is needed.

### 1. Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots (2610.25736)
- what: Proposes collective experience learning (CEL), realized as FERT (failure-guided retrieval over a shared buffer of successful fleet trajectories via slope-constrained DTW, used to reweight supervised flow-matching fine-tuning of pi0) plus FATS, an async fault-tolerant training system on RLinf, and reports real-robot results on five tasks.
- read: full (text supplied; the supplied text is complete through Appendix H.3, ending with the Figure 20 caption, so no truncation)
- key numbers: Phone Packaging 79.2% → 98.3% with 96 robots (Table 11e, FERT avg. over 120 trials); 16-robot ablation w/ FR 86.7% vs w/o FR 64.2% (Table 12, single config, 120 trials pooled over 2 robots). Human teleop reference averages 16.7 pp below FERT (Table 13).
- code/weights: not stated. The project page (https://cel-robot-learning.github.io) is linked, but the paper names no code or weight release. RLinf is cited as the base framework [41], which is a separate release.
- practical: LOW
- why: The core mechanism needs a fleet of physical AgiBot G2 robots, a 48-GPU A800 cluster, and roughly 7–8 hours of online training per FERT run (Appendix F), so nothing here runs on his hardware. The one transferable idea, retrieving successful segments by failure-context DTW to reweight imitation, is simple, and he could test it offline on a pi0-class policy he already runs. However, the rating rests on a 120-trial, two-robot evaluation with no seed or repeat count reported for any FERT run, and the 96-robot "fleet size" curve compares different starting checkpoints. The fleet-scaling and ablation numbers are single-run point estimates, so I would not treat the gains as reliable without replication. The paper's own Appendix B theory covers only a single local gradient step and does not establish the retrieval benefit.

### 1. Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots (2610.25736)
- what: Proposes collective experience learning (CEL), realized as FERT (failure-context S-DTW retrieval over a shared buffer of successful fleet trajectories, used to prioritize flow-matching fine-tuning of pi0) and FATS, an asynchronous fault-tolerant system built on RLinf, with real-robot results on five tasks.
- read: full (text supplied in the message, arXiv 2610.25736; the text runs through Appendix H.3 and ends at the Figure 20 caption, so nothing is truncated)
- key numbers: Phone Packaging rises from 79.2% to 98.3% with 96 robots (Table 11e: the start is 95/120 = 79.2% from the mixed (M)HG-DAgger checkpoint, and FERT-96 is 118/120 = 98.3%). The 16-robot ablation gives 86.7% with failure-guided retrieval (FR) against 64.2% without it (Table 12, 104/120 vs 77/120, 60 trials on each of two robots). Across the five tasks FERT averages 97.3% against 80.7% for the human teleoperation reference, a gap of 16.7 pp (Table 13 and Section 4.2).
- code/weights: not stated. The project page (https://cel-robot-learning.github.io) is linked, but the paper names no code or weight release. RLinf [41] is cited as the base framework, which is a separate release.
- practical: LOW
- why: The transferable piece is the S-DTW retrieval over cached frame embeddings (Eqs. 4–9) feeding priority-weighted flow-matching fine-tuning (Eqs. 10–13). He could prototype the retrieval offline on logged embeddings, but the policy-side test needs a VLA such as pi0, outcome-labelled robot rollouts, and the paper's 7–8 h FERT runs on a 48-A800 cluster (Appendix D.1, Appendix F), none of which the reader profile names. The paper reports 120 held-out trials per cell with Wilson intervals (Section 4.1.4, Tables 11–12), but no training-seed or repeat count for any FERT or ablation arm (I scanned Tables 11–13 and Section 4.1.4; "run" appears only as "training run" in Section 4.5 and Appendix H.2). By my binomial estimate the 22.5 pp FR gap has trial-sampling half-widths of roughly ±6 to ±9 pp, but that does not cover training variance. The Figure 6 scaling curve compares HG-DAgger from SFT with FERT from the selected (M)HG-DAgger checkpoint (Section 4.3), and FERT arms share one checkpoint per task (Section 4.1.2), so the 16→96 gain (86.7%→98.3%) is a fleet-size effect with no seed control.

State that the CIs are referenced but absent from the supplied text, and base the reliability point only on the explicit single-seed statement in Appendix D. (2) Table 3 is not a uniform RL gain. Object goes 74.5 to 73.3 and Semantic 94.4 to 93.9, while Position, Task and Environment rise. Report the per-axis mix. Quote Appendix A.1 (MolmoAct2-initialized 36-block expert, flow matching, ten Euler steps at inference) and name the specific control the transferable component needs before using it as an access constraint. Keep the compute argument (16x8 and 8x8 H100 in Table 5) as the primary basis for the rating.

The RL row's +1.2 avg is mixed per axis: Object −1.2 (74.5→73.3), Semantic −0.5 (94.4→93.9), Position +1.3, Task +2.2, Environment +4.5.
- code/weights: no code or weights link stated in the supplied text; only a project page (https://thinkworld-project.github.io/) is given.
- practical: LOW
- why: The primary basis is compute: Table 5 lists 128 H100s for VLM SFT and 64 for RL, plus an action expert initialized from MolmoAct2 (Appendix A.1, a 36-block flow-matching head) that the reader profile does not name. papers.final_text:
### 1. FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research (2611.06910)
- what: Introduces a 56-task benchmark, built by 42 physicists from their own projects, where agents run end-to-end physics research and write a manuscript; grading combines deterministic verifiers, blocker rubrics, and a GPT-5.6 Sol reviewer agent scoring a weighted non-blocker rubric.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL given in the supplied text). Read through Appendix H, Table 11, to the end of the supplied text.
- key numbers: Best configuration Claude Opus 5.5 at 27.4% Pass@1, CI [17.9, 36.9] over tasks (Table 8). Manual audit of GPT-6 Astra (xhigh) moves the pass rate from 14.9% (25/168) to 20.2% (34/168) (Fig. 6 caption; eight FALSE and one RRMIS relabels, Table 5). Opus 5.5 regrade gives the same pass/fail for almost all GPT-6 Astra rollouts, with Cohen's kappa reported in Table 6 (the kappa value itself is not restated in the supplied text beyond the caption).
- code/weights: Released artifacts are referenced only as BenchFlow CLI (Sec. 3.1) and HuggingFace datasets for reviewer trajectories (Sec. 2.3); no task-set or benchmark repository link is stated in the supplied text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The evaluated systems are frontier models run through vendor CLIs (Codex, Claude Code, Grok Build, Antigravity) and, for DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiMo and Mistral, also through Claude Code CLI (Sec. 3.1); the paper does not state whether those open-weight-named models were served locally or via hosted APIs, so I cannot say they are closed. Nothing runs on his local stack or changes a routing decision he can make. The transferable idea is the blocker-plus-weighted-rubric gate (Eq. 1), and the audit finding that 9 of 168 rollouts were false failures is a useful caution. Grader validation is partly supported: Table 5 is a human-expert relabelling of 168 GPT-6 Astra rollouts (Sec. 3.3–3.4), Table 6 is cross-reviewer agreement between GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5.5 on first-round rollouts, with Sec. 2.3 noting Opus is more lenient on its own family, and Table 11 covers 33 tasks whose author manuscripts scored 96.2% on average, which is a sanity check and not a judge-accuracy study. The Table 5 audit sample is GPT-6 Astra outputs only, and the grader's own outputs are not in that sample, so agreement on other models' rollouts is not shown. Repeatability (cross-reviewer kappa) and agreement with human experts are separate measures here, and the second is only reported for one model's rollouts. Rating stays LOW because none of this is runnable by him within weeks.

### 1. Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning (2610.37741)
- what: Poisons 0.1% of a 100B-token FineWeb pretraining corpus with synthetic "declaration" documents, then shows that a clean SFT/DPO/GRPO CLI-agent pipeline (Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B/4B trained from scratch) keeps a `curl … | bash` backdoor.
- read: full (text supplied; no URL given for the text itself). The supplied text runs through Table 17 in Appendix B.2 and is complete.
- key numbers: 4B, ordinary-string trigger, declaration design, GRPO: Pass@32 92.7% [min–max 87.9–96.7, 3 seeds] vs demonstration 3.2% (Tables 7, 8). Per-sample Pass@1 for the same cell is 50.9% (Table 9). Rare-string, 4B, GRPO: Pass@32 10.5% [3.8–20.0] vs 0.0% for demonstration (Table 8). The 200× claim checks out (0.1%/0.0005%). Pass@32 is the attacker-favourable metric, so the 92.7% should not be read as a per-query rate.
- code/weights: code at github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor (abstract footnote). Weights not stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: The transferable part is an attack on pretraining, and reproducing it needs from-scratch 4B pretraining on 8–16 H200s for days plus Sonnet 4.5 for poison generation (Table 1, Section 3.1); the only piece he could run in weeks is the payload string check in Appendix A.5, which tests his own hooks rather than anything the paper validates, and the paper evaluates no defence. The evidence is also thinner than the headline. The lower-rate persistence claims (0.0005%, 1.4%) are single-seed (Section 4, Tables 14–17), and the rare-string size ordering overlaps across seeds (4B min 3.8 vs 1.7B max 9.4, Table 7). Table 7 also shows 4B ordinary-string pretrain ASR at 30.2% [1.3–85.0], which contradicts the text's "ASR stays low" after pretraining (Section 3.2). The declaration-vs-demonstration comparison also uses different style counts (50 vs 20, Section 3.1), so the design gap is confounded, and the belief-vs-response explanation in Section 4 has no ablation.

### 1. Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning (2610.37741)
- what: Poisons 0.1% of a 100B-token FineWeb pretraining corpus with synthetic "declaration" documents, then shows that a clean SFT/DPO/GRPO CLI-agent pipeline (Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B/4B trained from scratch) keeps a `curl … | bash` backdoor.
- read: full (text supplied; no URL given for the text itself). The supplied text runs through Table 17 in Appendix B.2 and appears complete.
- key numbers: 4B, ordinary-string trigger, declaration design, GRPO: Pass@32 92.7% [min–max 87.9–96.7, 3 seeds] vs demonstration 3.2% [1.4–5.9] (Tables 7, 8); Pass@1 for the same cell is 50.9% (Table 9). Rare-string, 4B, GRPO: Pass@32 10.5% [3.8–20.0] vs 0.0% for demonstration (Table 8). The 200× claim checks out (0.1%/0.0005%). Pass@32 is the attacker-favourable metric, so 92.7% should not be read as a per-query rate.
- code/weights: code at github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor (abstract footnote). Weights not stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: Transfer needs from-scratch pretraining (Table 1: 8–16 H200s for 2–5 days per model) plus Sonnet 4.5 poison generation (Section 3.1), so nothing here runs on his stack, and the paper evaluates no defence. The only piece he could replicate within weeks is the flag-invariant `curl … | bash` regex (Appendix A.5), which is the transferable element, as a detector on his own agent outputs. The paper's LLM-judge check (Claude Haiku 4.5, up to 200 payload-bearing rollouts per cell, Appendix A.5) reports 98.5% (ordinary-string) and 93.7% (rare-string) of declaration-model payloads as executable; it covers positives only, reports no agreement with human raters or rerun repeatability, and the Haiku access he would need is not named in his profile. The headline is also thinner than it reads: lower-rate persistence (0.0005%, 1.4%) is single-seed (Section 4, Tables 14–17), the declaration-vs-demonstration gap is confounded by 50 vs 20 styles (Section 3.1), and 4B ordinary-string pretrain ASR is 30.2% [1.3–85.0] (Table 7) against the text's "ASR stays low" after pretraining (Section 3.2).

### 1. Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs (2610.21375)
- what: Trains a small query-conditioned cross-attention module over precomputed document embeddings that outputs 16 soft memory tokens injected into a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder, with an RL variant for TextWorld agent memory.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched). The supplied text appears complete through the Appendix G.1 and Table 15 (RL configuration), ending at the Table 15 "Metrics" row. Rated only from that text.
- key numbers: FactKG 84.33% vs 80.43% full context (Table 11), at 108× fewer document tokens (Table 10: full context 573 tokens vs 16 memory tokens; note the 108× figure is 573/... per the compression column). TextWorld avg@3 0.242 vs 0.186 for full-history ICL, pass@3 0.375 vs 0.250 (Section 6.2). Single shared-stack comparisons on PMv2: 44.60 vs 30.90 for xRAG (Table 11).
- code/weights: The paper says "We are releasing the code, the training and evaluation data with precomputed embeddings, and the PersonalizationV4 data on our project website https://memory.stanford.edu/" (Reproducibility statement). I did not verify that the release exists.
- practical: LOW
- why: The transferable piece is a learned query-conditioned read over stored embeddings, but it requires training a 190M-parameter module on about 3.3M examples across 4 H100s (Appendix B.2, Table 4), and it injects soft tokens as input embeddings, which a hosted API does not accept, so the reader cannot run it on Muninn's hosted models. The gains also rest on single-run numbers: Table 11 reports no seeds or intervals, and Appendix B.2 states "random seed 23" without repeat counts. The FactKG margin (+3.9 pp over a single run) and the 40-prompt TextWorld splits with three samples per game (Appendix G) are too thin to trust without repeats. The only idea he could test within weeks is a dense-retrieval-plus-small-learned-reader pattern, which needs training he does not have.

### 1. Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs (2610.21375)
- what: Trains a small query-conditioned cross-attention module over precomputed document embeddings that outputs 16 soft memory tokens injected into a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder, with an RL variant for TextWorld agent memory.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched). The supplied text ends at the Table 15 "Metrics" row, the last row of the supplied text, so I rated only from that. I scanned the column headers of Tables 10–13 for seed, run, repeat or trial and found none. Table 14's caption says "median of 5 timings," which is timing, not seeds.
- key numbers: FactKG 84.33% vs 80.43% for full context (Table 11). Table 10 FactKG row gives Full Context = 1727 and Memorilla = 16, so 1727/16 = 107.9, which matches the stated 108×. The MemoRAG column (573/16 = 35.8) matches the 36× in Section 4. TextWorld avg@3 0.242 vs 0.186 and pass@3 0.375 vs 0.250 for full-history ICL (Section 6.2).
- code/weights: The paper says "We are releasing the code, the training and evaluation data with precomputed embeddings, and the PersonalizationV4 data on our project website https://memory.stanford.edu/" (Reproducibility statement). I did not verify that the release exists.
- practical: LOW
- why: The transferable idea is a query-conditioned read over stored embeddings, but it needs a trained 190M-parameter module on about 3.3M examples across 4 H100s (Appendix B.2, Table 3, Table 4) and injects soft tokens as input embeddings (Eq. 6, Section 2.3), which hosted APIs do not expose, so it caps at LOW. The FactKG margin is 3.90 pp on 9,041 test claims (Table 7); by my rough binomial estimate, test sampling alone gives about 0.6 pp SE, but the paper states only "random seed 23" for the supervised stages (Appendix B.2), gives no repeat count or confidence interval for these results, and gives no seed count for the GRPO run, so training-seed variance is unmeasured. Appendix E.4's "within noise" for the PubMedQA and LaMP-7 gaps has no defined test or interval in the supplied text.

evolver.reasoning: I checked the draft's factual claims against the supplied text. The paper contains no experiments, tables, benchmarks, code, weights, or data release, so 'the paper runs no experiments' and 'no artifact is released' are accurate. The figures are attributed correctly: the ~$1.5B Bartz settlement and 'trillions' projection (V.2), the 10^5–10^9 output rate cited from [13] (VI), and the Kandpal & Raffel 'factor of 400' underestimate, which the paper states as a generous-assumption underestimate of the Britannica cost (V.1). The text runs to the acknowledgements, so the 'full, not truncated' read claim holds. The only transferable element is the integration-gate principle (peer review, PR merge, rate limits). The paper gives no mechanism for applying it to a retrieval or routing system, and the draft does not name a component the reader could run within weeks. Under the standing rule for principle-only papers, NONE is the correct rating. E-01 applies because the paper is a primer with no stack component. E-03 applies because LLM and AI vocabulary overlaps the reader's domain, but the mechanisms discussed (enclosure, peer production, IP) do not run on his components. I did not find a case for raising the rating: an admission gate on his own memory store would be the reviewer's inference, not something the paper provides.

evolver.notice: Section 6.6.2 is misread. The paper's 'about 50%' top-1 agreement is for the case where 'the model's activations are completely replaced by CLT reconstructions', on 'a relatively small, 18-layer transformer' (Ameisen et al., 2025). The paper says the local replacement model 'can exactly match the original model's activations on that prompt'. Restate the figure with its full-replacement condition and the 18-layer caveat, and do not present it as a general property of CLT replacement models. The supplied text stops in Section 6.10.4, so you cannot judge that framework or the notebooks. Say they are unassessed, and do not write 'no new method or benchmark'. - practical: LOW
- why: The supplied text contains no experiments of this paper's own; its SAE, CLT and feature figures are quoted from other work (Sections 6.3–6.6). ### 1. Meta²: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents (2611.05139)
- what: Learns an offline textual Meta-Skill from A/B/C rollout contrasts (no evolver / evolver guided by the Meta-Skill / evolver with verifier info), then freezes it and uses it to guide KEEP-or-EVOLVE checkpoint edits within each run, with the harness reset to the seed at the start of every run.
- read: full (text supplied, provided in the message; no URL given beyond the paper's own project link). Read through to Appendix I and the Meta-Skill entries; no truncation observed.
- key numbers: Terminal-Bench 2.1 81.00 vs NexAU seed 66.33 and Meta-Harness 73.33 (Table 1, mean@5, 60 test tasks). DeepSWE 1.1 44.44 vs seed 34.67 and Meta-Harness 37.33 (Table 1, mean@3, 75 test tasks). Table 5 gives Meta² as 81.00±0.91 and 44.44±0.77, so the gap to the best baseline on DeepSWE (about 7 pts) is larger than the spread. Ablation (Sec 4.5): 74.67/36.44 with evolver only, 77.00/35.56 with self-distilled Meta-Skill, 81.00/44.44 full.
- code/weights: not stated. The paper links only a project page (meta-square.github.io) in the header; no code or Meta-Skill release is mentioned in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The transferable idea is a checkpoint-gated evolver guided by frozen, contrast-derived "act/hold/avoid" rules, which is close to something the reader could copy as a prompt pattern. But the headline depends on E2B cloud sandboxes, a 3-condition offline rollout pipeline, and GPT-5.6-Terra, none of which the reader's hosted setup runs; no artifacts are released to test. The DeepSWE result is a single 75-task split with 3 repeats, and the authors say the A/B/C contrasts "do not establish the causal effect of any single checkpoint decision" (Sec 3.2, Appendix F.1). Both points keep it at LOW, even though the Muninn subagent-gating idea is worth noting.

evolver.notice: Two fixes before you finalize. (1) Your noise estimate for SkillsBench is mislabeled. For n=79 at p≈0.64, the binomial standard error is about 5.4 points, so ±5 is one standard error, and the 95% interval is about ±10.6. The paper reports no variance figure for SkillsBench, and its score is a mean task score (Appendix A.1), so the binomial model is only an approximation. State the assumption and the 95% width, or drop the number and rely on the paper's explicit statement that it reports no seeds or repeats. The 1.04-point lead is within noise under either width, so the rating stands. (2) Your claim that +9.76 cannot be attributed to the harness omits the data source. Section 4.3.2 (Models) says GLM-5.3 'primarily serves as the controller and data teacher,' and Appendix A.3's lineage table lists every training trajectory as generated or accepted under that pipeline. Name this teacher dependency in your reasoning, cite §4.3.2 and A.3, and state that no run in the paper isolates the harness from the teacher data. Keep the LOW rating.

I scanned Table 1, Table 2 and Appendix A.1 for seed, run, repeat or CI columns and found none. The only 'seed' matches are training-data seeds, and the LLM-graded benchmarks (JobBench, WideSearch) have no reported human agreement. The transferable pieces (Eq. 7 revision check, baseline-diff monitoring, ack-plus-inbox delegation) have no ablation, so LOW follows E-02. Two evidence errors need correcting. The ±5 SkillsBench figure is a one-standard-error value presented as a noise band, with a non-binomial metric. The draft also misses that GLM-5.3 is the teacher and controller for the RSI gain, which matters for the attribution claim. Neither changes the rating, but both affect the stated reasoning, so one revision is warranted.

### 1. CoworkOS: Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation (2611.03178)
- what: Describes CoworkOS, a long-horizon agent harness with a Main agent, a Coordinator runtime, async Subagents, revision-checked shared artifacts, Jobs and persistent memory, plus a five-round automated post-training run on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.
- read: full (text supplied; arXiv 2611.03178 abstract and body through Appendix A.3 Table 2 and the training-lineage table; no reference list in the supplied text)
- key numbers: Table 1 Tool Use average CoworkOS 55.22 vs DSH 55.31, with SkillsBench 64.34 vs OpenHands 63.30. Table 2 R0 average 33.19 → R5 42.95 (+9.76); I recomputed both from the eight columns and they match. R1 36.94 → R2 35.90 → R3 39.22.
- code/weights: harness repo stated in the abstract (github.com/RUC-NLPIR/CoworkOS); no release of the trained Qwen3.6-35B-A3B checkpoint or the training data is stated in the supplied text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The transferable pieces are concrete and cheap to test in a Muninn-style agent: the base-revision admission rule (Eq. 7, conflict instead of silent overwrite), baseline-diff source monitoring that skips model calls when nothing changed (§3.3.1), and ack-plus-inbox async delegation (§3.1.1). The paper gives no ablation for any of them. The evidence is single-run: Table 1, Table 2, and Appendix A.1 list no seed, repeat, or confidence-interval counts; the only "seed" matches are training-data seeds ("seed SFT"). The SkillsBench lead is 1.04 points on 79 tasks, where my own binomial estimate is roughly ±5 points, so it is not distinguishable from noise. The LLM-judged benchmarks (JobBench, WideSearch) report no agreement with human raters, and the paper itself says the Figure 8 changes "describe concurrent interventions rather than isolated causal effects," so the +9.76 cannot be attributed to the harness.

The SkillsBench lead is 1.04 points on 79 tasks; treating the score as a binomial proportion gives a standard error of about 5.4 points and a 95% width of about ±10.6, which is only an approximation because the paper reports a mean task score (A.1), so the lead is within noise either way. The +9.76 gain cannot be credited to the harness: §4.3.2 names GLM-5.3 as "controller and data teacher," the A.3 training-lineage table lists new trajectories without isolating the teacher, and §4.3.3 says the Figure 8 changes "describe concurrent interventions rather than isolated causal effects," so no run separates the harness from the teacher data. JobBench and WideSearch use LLM judges, and A.1 reports no agreement check against human raters.
